name: Aaron Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Gwen Talbot on her beef farm, a hundred and fifty suckler cows, that's cows that raise their own calves, and about a hundred and twenty hectares of grass we cut for hay and silage. In winter they're in the sheds, so it's feeding, bedding, checking for anything off its food. Summer is all hay. If the forecast gives you four dry days in June, you don't sleep.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the sale days, taking the weaned calves to market and seeing what they make. It's like a report card for the whole year. What wears me out is that I'm still learning cattle. Gwen can look at a cow and tell you she'll calve tonight. I need a camera in the shed and an alert on my phone, and even then I get it wrong.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You mentioned a camera. How much do you use technology?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: All day, honestly. I've got the calving camera on my phone, a weighing app that reads the scale by the crush, the steel pen you hold a cow in, and I use a chatbot most days for something, a weather question, a vet question, writing the sale entry. Gwen calls it my oracle. She's sixty-eight and she's come round to it, slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I already use it every day and it's just part of farming now. I'd probably tell people on the farming forum to try it for the paperwork, the cattle movement forms are a pain and it helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm on low pay with about three weeks of money in the bank, and a better search engine doesn't change that. Me and Rosa rent a little house in the village and she's a care assistant, so neither of us is rich. I need to earn more, and AI on its own won't do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at a side business. There's a lot of small fields round here nobody bales because it's not worth the big contractors' time. If I could get a second-hand baler on finance, I could do maybe forty small jobs a summer. I'd use the chatbot to work out the numbers before I talk to the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit impatient, maybe. I want to get on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the baler cost, and how would you pay for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decent second-hand one is about the price of a cheap car. I'd want Gwen to let me use her tractor in the evenings and pay her a bit per hour for it. If it works, it pays back in two summers. If it rains two summers running, I'm in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Rosa say about that risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say do the numbers twice. Then she'd say yes, because she knows I'll go mad otherwise. She's the careful one. I'm the one with a spreadsheet of hay prices from five years.

S0.say: I'd say I already use AI every day and it's just part of farming now. I'd tell people on the farming forum to try it for paperwork like cattle movement forms.
S0.think: I'm on low pay with about three weeks of money, and a better search engine doesn't change that. Rosa and I both need to earn more, and AI alone won't do it.
S0.do: Plans a side business baling small fields that big contractors ignore, financing a second-hand baler and renting Gwen's tractor in the evenings. Uses a chatbot to work out the numbers before going to the bank.
S0.feel: Calm, with an impatient wish to get on.
S0.quote: If it works, it pays back in two summers. If it rains two summers running, I'm in trouble.
S0.fieldNote: He has a business plan ready before I've finished the first scenario. He's comfortable taking on debt, unlike most in this group with thin savings, and his partner acts as the brake. The 'oracle' nickname from his boss showed the gap between them, now narrowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a bad deal for young people, and farming's already short of them. But I'd also say the ones who learn the tools will be fine. That's what I'd tell my younger cousin, who wants to do agricultural college.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me. Slow means I've got years, and I'm already the young one who knows the tech. When Gwen retires, whoever takes over will want someone who knows both the cows and the apps. That's me if I don't mess it up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Do the baling business, start small. Take the cattle course at the college, the one on breeding and records, because I'm weak on breeding. Try to get Gwen to let me run the breeding records properly on the computer so I learn it from the inside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Good, actually. This is my best one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your cousin, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the animals first and the phone second. Everyone our age has the phone. Not many can tell a sick calf from a sleepy one, and the camera can't either, not reliably. That's what gets you hired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'if I don't mess it up'. What could mess it up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Taking on too much. Baler debt, college, the farm, all at once, and then one bad winter with the cattle. I've seen people burn out. Well, one, a friend from school, he had three jobs and he's driving a forklift now.

S1.say: I'd say it's a bad deal for young people, and farming is already short of them. But the ones who learn the tools will be fine.
S1.think: Honestly I think slow change is good for me, because I'm already the young one who knows the tech. When Gwen retires, the next owner will want someone who knows both cows and apps.
S1.do: Starts the baling business small and takes the college course on cattle breeding and records. Asks Gwen to let him run the breeding records on the computer.
S1.feel: Calm and positive. He called it his best scenario.
S1.quote: Not many can tell a sick calf from a sleepy one, and the camera can't either, not reliably.
S1.fieldNote: He was openly optimistic and saw himself as the bridge between an older owner and new tools. The advice to his cousin, animals first, phone second, was more careful than his own instincts. He named burnout as his main risk, using a school friend as the warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people losing office jobs need help, and some of them should look at farming, honestly. There's work. It's not well paid, but it's real. I'd keep out of the shouting about politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's mostly fine for me. Maybe slightly good, because the AI agents might do all the government forms for farms, and that frees Gwen up. The thing that could hurt is beef prices, if lots of people lose office pay and stop buying steak.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch the cattle prices at market every week, I already track them. If they drop, I'd push the baling harder, because hay sells whatever happens. I'd also try selling some beef boxes straight to people, half a cow's worth split into family packs, using the AI to do the website.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit. Mainly about prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Gwen go along with selling beef boxes direct?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd hate the idea at first. She's sold through the market for forty years. But if I showed her the numbers, the extra money per animal, she'd say try ten. That's how she works, try ten first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rosa's sister, who works at the bank in town. And the auction mart, actually, the office side, they've got five people doing paperwork. If that goes, the market might close, and then where do we sell?

S2.say: I'd say people losing office jobs need help, and some should look at farming because there's real work. I'd stay out of the political shouting.
S2.think: Privately it's mostly fine and maybe slightly good, if AI agents handle the government forms. The risk is beef prices dropping if office workers stop buying steak.
S2.do: Tracks weekly cattle prices at market and pushes the baling business harder if they fall. Starts selling beef boxes direct to families, using AI to build the website, beginning with ten animals if Gwen agrees.
S2.feel: A little uneasy, mainly about prices.
S2.quote: She's sold through the market for forty years. But if I showed her the numbers, the extra money per animal, she'd say try ten.
S2.fieldNote: He traced office job losses to steak sales within seconds, and had two hedges ready. A sharp second-order worry: the auction mart's office staff, and whether the market itself survives. Pragmatic and middle-ground on politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farming's a good place to be in this one, and I'd say it a bit too loud, probably. I'd also say the government needs to sort out who gets the money, without killing off the companies. Both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job's okay, my rent isn't. If house prices boom, the landlord either sells our place or puts the rent up by a lot. And Rosa's care home, the managers and admin might go, which means more work for her for the same pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Push the beef boxes, because if people with shares are getting rich, some of them want nice local beef. I'd go after those customers on purpose. Keep the baling. Put every spare bit into a savings account, even if it's small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Nervous about rent, but there's money moving and I'd want to catch some.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd sell beef to the people getting rich. How does that sit with you, when others are losing jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, honestly, I'm not proud of that. I can't fix the economy. I can sell a good box of beef to someone who can afford it and pay my rent. That's my bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the landlord sells?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd look for a farm cottage, which is a tied house, comes with a job, so I'd be stuck. Or move in with Rosa's parents for six months, which we'd survive, just. Her dad watches the news at full volume.

S3.say: I'd say farming is a good place to be in this one, and that the government should sort out who gets the gains without killing off companies. I'd probably say it a bit too loudly.
S3.think: My job's okay but my rent isn't, because a booming housing market means the landlord sells or raises the rent. Rosa's care home could also lose admin staff, piling more work on her for the same pay.
S3.do: Targets beef box sales at people who are doing well from rising shares, keeps the baling business going and saves every spare bit. Plans for a tied farm cottage or six months with Rosa's parents if the landlord sells.
S3.feel: Uneasy about rent, but alert to the money moving and keen to catch some.
S3.quote: I can't fix the economy. I can sell a good box of beef to someone who can afford it and pay my rent. That's my bit.
S3.fieldNote: He was candid that he'd sell to the winners without much guilt, a pragmatic rather than political answer. The housing worry showed up again, as it has across this group. He's alert to Rosa's work getting heavier even in a scenario that spares physical jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks for staying with me. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farms have had machines for a hundred years and we're still here. I'd say the clever farms will use robots and keep good people. That's what I'd say at market, and I'd mean it about half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The other half, off the record, is that feeding and bedding is exactly what a robot would do first. There are already feed robots that drive round sheds on their own pushing silage up to the cows. Gwen wouldn't buy one, but the next owner would. I'd rather owe money on a robot than wait to be told I'm not needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get in early. Look at whether I could run a robot service myself, feed pushers or drone checks for small farms that can't afford to buy. Talk to the bank, talk to the dealers. I'd sell the baler if I had to, to fund it. And I'd tell Rosa to look hard at her care home, because robots in care homes is on your card too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more awake than scared. Like the night before a big sale.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: That's a lot of debt with three weeks of savings. What if it went wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we'd be in real trouble, I won't pretend. Rosa would carry us for a while. But staying still in this picture is also a risk, it's just a quieter one. I'd rather lose trying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to the cattle side, do you think, the part you said needs a good eye?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit I'd hang onto. Robots can push feed, but a cow calving wrong at night still needs someone who's not scared to put their arm in. Maybe that's my job in five years. Fewer hours, but the hours that count.

S4.say: I'd say farms have had machines for a hundred years and we're still here, and clever farms will use robots and keep good people. I'd say that at market and mean about half of it.
S4.think: Feeding and bedding is exactly what a robot would do first, and feed robots that drive round sheds already exist. I'd rather owe money on a robot than wait to be told I'm not needed.
S4.do: Explores running a robot or drone service for small farms that can't afford to buy, talking to the bank and dealers and selling the baler if needed. Warns Rosa to watch for robots in her care home.
S4.feel: Anxious, but more awake than scared, like the night before a big sale.
S4.quote: I'd rather owe money on a robot than wait to be told I'm not needed.
S4.fieldNote: He told me straight that he'd mean only half his public line, which is a rare level of self-awareness. His instinct is to borrow and move first, even with almost no savings. He pinned his long-term value on night calving, the moment that needs a person.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots one, because it hits me and Rosa at the same time, the farm and the care home. What would help is cheap loans for young people to buy into the new kit, so it's not only the big farms that own the robots. And courses that are short and practical, not two years.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the auction marts. They're the centre of farming round here, where you hear everything and see everyone. If the paperwork goes AI and the selling goes online, the marts close, and farmers just sit alone on their farms. That's not good for anyone's head.

headlineQuote: I'd rather owe money on a robot than wait to be told I'm not needed.
portrait: Aaron Torres is a 27-year-old stockman on a 150-cow beef farm run by a 68-year-old owner who calls his chatbot 'the oracle'. He uses AI tools daily, rents a small house with his partner Rosa, a care assistant, and has about three weeks of savings, yet he is the most willing in this group to borrow and start something. Across the scenarios he hedges with a baling business, beef boxes sold direct, and finally a robot service for small farms. His politics are pragmatic and middle-ground, and he admits selling to the winners without much guilt. He worries most when robots threaten both his work and Rosa's care home at once.
biggestWorry: The fast robots scenario, because it would hit his farm work and his partner's care home job at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap loans so young people can buy into new machinery, and short, practical courses rather than long ones.
